austria.intro:
Austria is a small Alpine country with grand cities, lakes, mountains and a strong tradition of hospitality. Its food mixes Central European comfort dishes with famous cakes and fine wines.

This page explains what Austria is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Austria is known for Vienna's palaces and music, Salzburg's baroque old town, the Alps and winter sports. Its coffee house culture is recognized by UNESCO, and its villages and lakes draw hikers and skiers throughout the year.

Meals tend to be generous, and many regions have their own traditions, from Tyrolean mountain cooking to Styrian pumpkin seed oil.

Wiener schnitzel, a thin breaded veal or pork cutlet, is the national dish, and Tafelspitz, boiled beef with horseradish, is a Viennese classic. Look also for goulash, dumplings, Kaesespaetzle, a cheesy noodle dish, and roasted pork with cabbage.

Desserts are famous: apple strudel, Sachertorte, Kaiserschmarrn, a torn sweet pancake, and Salzburger Nockerl. Austria also produces Gruener Veltliner and other white wines.

Vienna offers palaces, opera and coffee houses, Salzburg has Mozart's birthplace and a fortress, and Innsbruck sits among mountains. Hallstatt is a picturesque lake village, and Graz has a lively old town.

In winter, the Tyrol and Vorarlberg offer top skiing, while in summer the lakes of Carinthia are popular for swimming.

austria/carinthia.intro:
Carinthia is the southernmost Austrian state, with warm lakes, forests and mountains on the border with Italy and Slovenia.

This page explains what Carinthia is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The state is known for its lakes, such as the Woerthersee, which warm up enough for swimming in summer. Its Alpine peaks and the Grossglockner High Alpine Road draw visitors, and its position gives a gentle blend of Austrian, Italian and Slovenian influences.

Small villages, lakeside promenades and castles add to the charm.

Kaernten Kasnudeln, large dumplings filled with cheese and herbs, are the regional specialty. Look for lake fish, smoked meats, hearty soups and sweet dishes. Reindling, a yeast cake with raisins and cinnamon, is traditional at festivals.

The region's food shows Italian touches, such as pasta and polenta, and local cheese and farm produce are widely used.

The lakes, with their boat trips and beaches, are the main draw. Klagenfurt is the capital, and Villach has thermal baths. The Grossglockner road and the Nockberge mountains offer drives and hikes.

Hohe Tauern National Park protects glaciers and waterfalls.

austria/carinthia/klagenfurt.intro:
Klagenfurt is the capital of Carinthia, set at the eastern end of the Woerthersee. Its old town and lake life give it a relaxed, sunny character.

This page explains what Klagenfurt is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for its lake beaches, its Renaissance old town and the Lindwurm fountain, a dragon statue that is the city's symbol. A short walk from the center leads to the lake.

The climate is mild, and cafes spill onto the squares in summer.

Try Kasnudeln, lake fish such as whitefish and trout, smoked ham and hearty soups. Cafes serve coffee with Reindling or strudel, and the cooking shows Italian and Slovenian touches. Markets sell local cheese, vegetables and pumpkin seed oil.

Beer gardens and lakeside terraces are popular in warm months.

The Neuer Platz and the Lindwurm fountain, the Landhaus courtyard and the Woerthersee beaches are the highlights. Minimundus, a miniature world park, is popular with families. Pyramidenkogel, a tall tower, offers lake views.

The Maria Saal church and Hochosterwitz Castle are nearby.

Book ahead on summer weekends.

Summer is warm and sunny, and lake swimming is easy. Many shops close on Sundays. A rental bike is a good way to travel along the lake.

austria/salzburg.intro:
The state of Salzburg stretches from the famous city to Alpine valleys, lakes and ski resorts. It has a strong tradition of music, salt mining and mountain cooking.

This page explains what Salzburg is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The state is known for the city of Salzburg, Mozart's birthplace, and for the Salzkammergut lake region and the Hohe Tauern mountains. The salt mines gave the area its name and wealth, and visitors can tour old mines.

Winter brings skiing at resorts such as Saalbach and Zell am See.

Salzburger Nockerl, a sweet, fluffy soufflé, is the signature dessert, and Mozartkugeln are famous chocolates. Savory favorites include Kaesespaetzle, pork roast, trout and rich soups. Beer brewed at old abbeys is a local pride.

Mountain huts serve simple, hearty meals such as Kaiserschmarrn.

Salzburg's old town and fortress, the Mirabell gardens and Mozart sites are popular. The Hallein salt mines, the Werfen ice caves and the lakes of the Salzkammergut offer excursions.

The Grossglockner High Alpine Road and the Krimml waterfalls are scenic.

austria/salzburg/salzburg.intro:
Salzburg is a baroque city on the Salzach river, framed by mountains. It is one of the most visited cities in Austria, with cafes, beer halls and elegant restaurants.

This page explains what Salzburg is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known as Mozart's birthplace, for the Sound of Music film locations and for the annual Salzburg Festival. The old town is a World Heritage site, and the Hohensalzburg fortress watches over it.

The narrow lanes, guild signs and courtyards make walking a pleasure.

Try Salzburger Nockerl, a giant sweet soufflé, Mozartkugeln chocolates, Wiener schnitzel and hearty Austrian dishes such as goulash and dumplings. Brewery taverns serve beer with pork roast and pretzels, and coffee houses offer cakes.

A food market on Thursday mornings and Saturday sells local produce and snacks.

Getreidegasse, the Cathedral, the Mirabell Palace gardens and Hohensalzburg are the main sights. The Mozart birthplace museum, the St. Peter's Abbey and Hellbrunn Palace trick fountains are also popular.

Day trips go to the lakes of the Salzkammergut and the Berchtesgaden area.

The city can be crowded in summer. Rain is frequent, so keep a jacket handy. Many restaurants have a break in the afternoon, so check hours.

Styria is called the green heart of Austria, with forested hills, vineyards and a strong food culture based on local farms.

This page explains what Styria is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The state is known for its wine roads in the south, its pumpkin fields and its capital Graz, a university city with a UNESCO listed old town. The mountains in the north offer hiking and skiing.

The region has long been known for its culinary traditions.

Styrian pumpkin seed oil is a dark, nutty oil drizzled on salads, soups and even ice cream. Other specialties include roasted chicken, Backhendl, fried pork, buckwheat dishes and Styrian wines, especially Sauvignon Blanc and Welschriesling.

Buschenschank taverns serve cold platters and wine from their own farms.

Graz has an old town, a clock tower and a modern art museum. The south Styrian wine road is lovely for drives and tastings, and the Erzberg mine and the Eisenerz area show mining history.

Schladming and the Dachstein offer mountain activities.

Autumn is a good time for wine and food festivals. Many farm taverns open only on certain days. A car helps if you want to explore the wine roads.

austria/styria/graz.intro:
Graz is Austria's second largest city, with a UNESCO old town, a hilltop clock tower and a lively student population. It is known as a city of culinary delights.

This page explains what Graz is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Schlossberg hill with its clock tower, the Kunsthaus modern art gallery, nicknamed the friendly alien, and an old town with red roofs and courtyards. Students keep the city lively.

Graz has been named a city of culinary delights, and farm markets are central to local life.

Look for Styrian dishes, with pumpkin seed oil, Backhendl, Styrian beef and local wines. The Kaiser Josef market sells regional produce, and the farmers market at Lendplatz is lively. Cafes serve strudel, cakes and strong coffee.

Craft beer and creative menus are growing in popularity.

The Schlossberg, the Uhrturm, the Hauptplatz, the Eggenberg Palace and the Murinsel, an island in the river, are popular. The Kunsthaus and the Old Town are central, and wine country is a short ride away.

The Austrian Open Air Museum is nearby.

Look for places that highlight regional produce, and book ahead for evenings.

The city is walkable. Many places close on Sundays. In winter, Christmas markets are lovely.

austria/tyrol.intro:
Tyrol is the heartland of Alpine tourism in Austria, with high peaks, ski resorts and traditional villages.

This page explains what Tyrol is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The state is known for winter sports, with resorts such as Kitzbuehel, St. Anton and Soelden, and for its summer hiking and cycling. Innsbruck, the capital, sits among mountains and has a charming old town.

Tyrolean traditions, such as folk music, costumes and festivals, remain strong.

Tyrolean cooking is hearty: Kaesespaetzle, Tiroler Groestl, a fried potato and meat dish, Knoedel dumplings, and Speck, a smoked ham. Mountain huts serve Kaiserschmarrn and Germknoedel, a sweet yeast dumpling with poppy seeds.

Local cheeses, schnapps and beer complete the table.

Innsbruck offers the Golden Roof and cable cars up to the mountains. Kitzbuehel has a historic town and ski slopes, and the Zillertal and Stubai valleys have glaciers and hiking. Achensee is the largest lake in Tyrol.

The Swarovski Crystal Worlds in Wattens is also popular.

austria/tyrol/innsbruck.intro:
Innsbruck is a city in a valley surrounded by high peaks. It combines a medieval old town with quick access to ski slopes and hiking trails.

This page explains what Innsbruck is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Golden Roof, its colorful riverside houses and the Nordkette mountains that rise right above the town. It hosted two Winter Olympic Games, and the cable car takes you from the center to alpine views in minutes.

The old town is small and walkable, with arcades, cafes and shops.

Try Tyrolean specialties such as Kaesespaetzle, Tiroler Groestl, Knoedel and Speck. Mountain restaurants serve Kaiserschmarrn, and traditional inns serve roast pork and goulash. Strudel and Tyrolean cakes are widely available.

Markets and delis sell cheese and cured meats.

The Golden Roof, the Hofburg, the Ambras Castle and the Nordkette cable car are popular. The Bergisel ski jump has views of the city, and the Swarovski Crystal Worlds is nearby.

Day trips go to the Stubai glacier and the Alpine villages.

Plan around weather. In winter, book ahead for ski days. The city can be rainy, so a jacket is useful.

austria/tyrol/kitzbuhel.intro:
Kitzbuehel is a small medieval town in the Tyrol, known worldwide for skiing and for a stylish yet traditional atmosphere.

This page explains what Kitzbühel is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The town is known for the Hahnenkamm downhill ski race, one of the toughest in the world, and for its colorful old town with painted houses. In summer, it is a base for hiking, cycling and golf.

The town has a lively evening scene, with bars and mountain huts.

Dining ranges from rustic mountain huts to refined restaurants. Look for Tyrolean dishes such as Kaesespaetzle, Speck, goulash and Kaiserschmarrn, along with local game and trout. Cafes serve cakes and hot chocolate.

After skiing, apres ski places serve warm drinks and snacks.

The Hahnenkamm and Kitzbueheler Horn offer ski slopes in winter and hikes in summer. The old town, the Schwarzsee lake and the museum are popular. The Kitzbueheler Alps have many scenic trails.

The Kaiser mountains are nearby.

Upper Austria lies north of the Alps, with the Salzkammergut lake district, the Danube valley and its capital Linz.

sections.h2: What Upper Austria is known for
sections.body:
The state is known for the Hallstatt region, with its lakes and mountains, for the Danube cycle path and for the city of Linz. The area has a long history of salt mining and rural traditions.

Its food leans toward hearty farm cooking, dumplings and sweet baking.

Look for Knoedel dumplings, roasted meats, fresh lake fish and cakes. The Linzer Torte, a nut and jam tart, is the most famous local sweet. Cider and beer are traditional drinks, and farm shops sell cheese and bread.

Cafes and bakeries are excellent for afternoon coffee.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Upper Austria
sections.body:
Hallstatt, with its lakeside setting, and the Dachstein caves are the highlights. Linz has the Ars Electronica Center and the Pöstlingberg. The lakes of Traunsee and Attersee are good for swimming and boat rides.

The Danube path is a popular cycle route.

austria/upper-austria/hallstatt-area.intro:
Hallstatt sits on a lake beneath steep mountains and is one of the most photographed villages in Europe. The area also includes lake towns and mountain trails around it.

This page explains what the Hallstatt area is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What the Hallstatt area is known for
sections.body:
The village is known for its houses stacked along the lake, its salt mine, the oldest in the world, and its World Heritage listing. The setting, with mist rising over the water, draws many visitors.

The Dachstein mountains offer cable cars, ice caves and hiking trails.

Lake fish such as char and whitefish, served grilled or fried, are the local specialty. Try Knoedel, roasted meats, Kaiserschmarrn and strudel. Cafes along the lake serve cakes and coffee with views.

Heuriger and farm shops sell cheese and smoked products.

sections.h2: Places to visit in the Hallstatt area
sections.body:
The salt mine and its funicular, the Skywalk viewing platform, the lakeside promenade and the Dachstein ice caves are the main sights. Boat rides and walks around the lake are relaxing.

Nearby Gosau, Bad Goisern and the Traunsee area offer quieter alternatives.

Visit early or late in the day to avoid crowds. Parking is limited, so use public transport or park outside the village. Weather can be rainy.

austria/upper-austria/linz.intro:
Linz is a city on the Danube with an industrial past and a modern cultural scene. It is the home of the original Linzer Torte.

This page explains what Linz is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Ars Electronica Center, a museum of art and technology, its riverside promenades and the Pöstlingberg church on a hill above. A tram climbs up the hill for city views.

The city has a friendly, quiet feel, with cafes and gardens by the river.

The Linzer Torte, a nut pastry with a lattice top and currant jam, is the local specialty, and cafes serve it with coffee. Other favorites include roasted meats, dumplings, Danube fish and hearty soups.

Beer and cider are common drinks, and the farmers markets sell regional products.

The Hauptplatz, the Ars Electronica Center, the Lentos art museum and the Pöstlingberg tram are highlights. The Danube cycle path starts nearby, and the St. Florian monastery and Mauthausen memorial are day trips.

The lakes of the Salzkammergut are an hour away.

For a view, choose a place on the Pöstlingberg.

The city is calm in the evenings, and many places close early. Check hours, especially on Sundays.

austria/vienna.intro:
Vienna is both the capital of Austria and one of its states, a grand city with palaces, opera houses and a food scene that ranges from coffee houses to wine taverns.

This page explains what Vienna is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Schoenbrunn and Belvedere palaces, the State Opera and its musical heritage, linked to Mozart, Beethoven and Strauss. The coffee house tradition is a cultural treasure, and wine grown within the city limits is served in local taverns.

Its museums and parks give the city a cultured, relaxed feel.

Wiener schnitzel is the icon, served with potato salad and a slice of lemon. Tafelspitz, goulash and Kaesespaetzle are other classics, and sausage stands serve Käsekrainer. Desserts include Sachertorte, apple strudel and Kaiserschmarrn.

Coffee comes in many styles, such as the Melange, and young white wine is served in Heuriger taverns.

Schoenbrunn Palace, the Hofburg, St. Stephen's Cathedral, the Naschmarkt and the Prater with its giant wheel are classic. The museum quarter offers art, and the Ringstrasse is a grand boulevard for walks.

The Wachau valley is a day trip for wine and castles.

Book ahead for dinner and for popular cafes on weekends.

Tipping around 10 percent is customary. Sundays are quiet, with many shops closed. Public transport is excellent and cheap for visitors.

austria/vienna/vienna.intro:
Vienna is Austria's capital, known for its imperial history, its music and its dining traditions. It regularly ranks among the most liveable cities in the world.

This page explains what Vienna is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for Schoenbrunn and Belvedere palaces, the Opera, St. Stephen's Cathedral and the Ringstrasse. Its coffee house culture is recognized by UNESCO, and people linger for hours over a cup and a newspaper.

It also has a lively modern scene in neighborhoods such as the Museum Quarter and Neubau.

A proper Wiener schnitzel is cut thin, breaded and fried in butter. Tafelspitz, goulash, Kaesespaetzle and fried chicken are other classics. Sausages at street stands are a casual meal, and the Naschmarkt has international food stalls.

Sachertorte, strudel, Kaiserschmarrn and Marillenknoedel, apricot dumplings, are the sweet highlights.

Visit Schoenbrunn Palace, the Hofburg, St. Stephen's Cathedral and the Belvedere. The Naschmarkt, the Prater wheel and the Museum Quarter are popular. The Vienna Woods and vineyards are easy to reach by tram.

In December, Christmas markets fill the squares.

Choose a coffee house for a long breakfast or afternoon cake, a Beisl for a local meal and a Heuriger in the suburbs for wine. Book ahead on weekends and in peak season.

Tipping about 10 percent is normal, usually by rounding up. Many places close on Sundays, so plan ahead. Tap water is excellent and free.

austria/vorarlberg.intro:
Vorarlberg is the westernmost Austrian state, with Lake Constance, the Bregenz Forest and the Arlberg ski region.

This page explains what Vorarlberg is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The state is known for Lake Constance, the Bregenz Festival with its floating stage, and the ski resorts of Lech and Zuers. Its villages preserve a distinct Alemannic culture and architecture.

The region has a strong reputation for quality food and for cheese.

Vorarlberg is known for its mountain cheeses, such as Bergkaese and Alpkaese, and for Kaesespaetzle, Kaesknoepfle and Riebel, a corn dish. Lake fish such as whitefish are popular on the shore, and regional wines and beers are widely served.

Bakeries sell Bregenzerwald breads and sweet specialties.

Bregenz has the lake promenade, the Pfaender cable car and the festival stage. Dornbirn offers museums and markets, and the Bregenz Forest has cheese farms and wooden architecture. Lech and Arlberg are for skiing.

The Montafon valley is good for hiking.

Lakeside restaurants are popular in summer.

Winter is busy in the ski areas, and summer is good for the lake and hiking. Book ahead during the Bregenz Festival.

austria/vorarlberg/bregenz.intro:
Bregenz is a small city on the eastern shore of Lake Constance, with mountain views, a lakeside promenade and an old town on the hill.

This page explains what Bregenz is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Bregenz Festival, an opera event with a stage built on the lake, and for the Pfaender cable car, which lifts you quickly to mountain views over the lake. The Kunsthaus Bregenz is a striking modern art museum.

The old town has quiet lanes and a clock tower.

Lake fish such as whitefish and perch, usually pan fried, are the local favorite. Try Kaesespaetzle, local cheeses, and regional wines and beers. Cafes serve cake, coffee and ice cream on the promenade.

Bakeries sell local bread and sweets.

The lake promenade, the Pfaender cable car, the old town and the Kunsthaus are popular. In summer, boat trips cross the lake to Germany and Switzerland.

The Bregenz Forest is close for hiking and cheese tasting.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Bregenz
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Lakeside places offer views but get busy in summer. During the festival, book well ahead.

The summer festival runs in July and August. The weather is mild, and the lake is good for swimming. Many places close on Sundays.
